events.title: Japan and World Food Programme Partner to Provide Nutritious School Meals for 50,000 Young Children in Lesotho
events.summary: Countries: Lesotho, Japan Source: World Food Programme MASERU, Lesotho – The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) welcomes a JPY 200 million contribution, equivalent to USD 1.2 million, from the Government of Japan to provide nutritious school meals to 50,000 children in early childhood care and development centres across Lesotho. The contribution comes as malnutrition remains a serious concern in Lesotho, where 36 percent of children under 5 are stunted. School meals provide a vital safety net for young children, particularly in rural communities, while supporting healthier diets, regular attendance and learning. Speaking at a ceremony to announce the contribution, His Excellency Shimizu Fumio, Ambassador of Japan to Lesotho said: “For a child, a meal is about far more than simply addressing hunger. It provides the energy to learn, the nourishment to grow, and the opportunity to fully participate in school and in the community. Executive Summary Over time, coordinated humanitarian response in Northeast Nigeria has progressed with minimal multi-year evidence and insight captured across annual datasets. This retrospective longitudinal analysis of secondary humanitarian datasets synthesizes five years of UNOCHA needs and planning datasets from 2022 to 2026 to extract actionable lessons for the future. An examination of needs and demographic trends reveals that the crisis remains protracted, with deep vulnerabilities persisting across total People in Need (PiN). Over the five-year period, Borno consistently remained the epicenter of the crisis, while Yobe’s caseload held steady despite tighter counting boundaries in 2026. Press release Yemen Published 26. Nov 2026 Yemen entered this year as one of the most profound and most neglected humanitarian crises. Renewed fighting and airstrikes along multiple frontlines have uprooted hundreds of thousands of people. Despite shocking levels of suffering, the international response has withered, and conflict and civilian harm continues unabated. In the north, home to most of the country’s population, a handful of overstretched and underfunded national and international organisations are the only remaining lifeline to millions in need. Severe funding reductions, sanctions, and the UN’s ongoing pause in its operations following detention of their aid workers have all contributed to a collapsing humanitarian response, compounded by the insecurity and access constraints. “The situation across the country was already catastrophic, with long-term displacement and long-term humanitarian needs growing almost entirely out of sight,” said Egeland. “But now fighting has again displaced entire communities, while disrupted supply routes have driven up food and fuel prices. events.title: Afghanistan: Impact of the Bans and Restrictions on Women Working for NGOs, INGOs and the UN - Round 16 (October 2026)
events.summary: Country: Afghanistan Sources: Asia Pacific Gender in Humanitarian Action Working Group, UN Women Please refer to the attached Infographic. This snapshot presents findings from the sixteenth round of the GCG and HAWG survey on the impact of the bans and other gender-related restrictions on Afghan women working for NGOs, INGOs and the UN. Responses were collected from 7 to 26 October 2026 from 90 organizations: 72 NNGOs and CSOs (62 of them WLOs), 10 INGOs and 8 UN agencies. This round has more respondents working on GBV (60%, from 44% in June) and on human rights and gender equality (69%, from 59%). Restrictions on women's participation in humanitarian and BHN operations remain widespread, despite a decline in reports of new formal instructions. While 36% of organizations reported no new instructions or impediments, practical barriers persist: half report that women staff cannot report to the office in some provinces, and 32% report women staff stopped by the PVPV on the way to work, the highest level across all rounds. Only 42% remain fully operating with women and men, and fewer hold agreements with the DfA for women to work at project locations and offices. With 66% accepting DfA conditions to keep operating, the findings suggest a shift from new formal restrictions towards more persistent enforcement.

Uganda National Baseline Survey on School Feeding (December 2025)
events.summary: Country: Uganda Source: Government of Uganda Please refer to the attached file. Uganda’s National Baseline Survey on School Feeding provides a comprehensive national picture of the coverage, quality and delivery of school meals in primary schools. Led by the Ministry of Education and Sports , the survey establishes an important evidence base to inform policy, programming, investment and future monitoring of school feeding across the country. The findings show that 46 percent of primary school learners receive school meals , with significant disparities across regions and school types. Coverage is highest in Karamoja, Kampala and Buganda North , and lowest in Tooro, Ankole and West Nile , while rural, public and day schools generally have lower coverage. Critically, around 30 percent of learners do not eat any meal while at school , highlighting the continued challenge of hunger during the school day. The report also identifies gaps in dietary diversity, financing, procurement, infrastructure and management, and recommends expanding coverage in underserved areas, improving the nutritional quality of meals, strengthening local procurement and financing, and integrating school feeding more systematically into national education planning and monitoring.

events.title: Brazil: PAHO calls for stronger surveillance amid increase in mpox cases in the Americas
events.summary: Countries: Brazil, World Source: Pan American Health Organization Washington, D.C., 25 November 2026 (PAHO) – The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) is urging countries in the Americas to strengthen surveillance, laboratory capacity and prevention measures, including vaccination, in response to a surge in mpox cases in several countries of the Region. In an Epidemiological Alert issued on 24 November, PAHO highlights an increase in cases since epidemiological week 39 of 2026, primarily in Brazil, alongside the growing detection of mpox clade Ib in the Region. From January to November 2026, 13 countries reported 3,269 confirmed cases and four deaths. Since 2022, 76,084 cases and 202 deaths have been reported across 31 countries and territories in the Americas. Brazil has reported 1,325 cases in 2026, including one death, with an increase since September. Mpox continues to disproportionately affect men who have sex with men. Of the 114 reported mpox deaths for which HIV status was known, 111 (97%) were among people with HIV. PAHO is urging health authorities to strengthen epidemiological and genomic surveillance to ensure timely detection and investigation of cases, monitor changes in transmission patterns, and reinforce targeted prevention and control measures, including vaccination, particularly among populations at increased risk. What is mpox and how can it be prevented? Mpox is an infectious disease caused by the mpox virus. It can spread through close physical contact with someone who has the infection, including skin-to-skin and intimate contact, as well as through contact with contaminated materials such as clothing and bedding. Abstract/Description Flood Early Warning Bulletins translate forecasts into clear, timely, actionable information for preparedness, anticipatory action, and emergency response. By presenting expected conditions, potential impacts, and recommended actions in a standard format, they help government agencies, humanitarian organizations, and at-risk communities coordinate decisions before floods occur. Yet fragmented datasets, disconnected modelling workflows, and manual processes often delay bulletins and shorten the time available to protect lives, livelihoods, and infrastructure. events.title: World: How can we support survivors of gender-based violence?

Recognizing this reality, designing solutions to protect them, and committing to ways of working that do not perpetuate threats to women's lives and well-being is one of our priorities. In this article, we share recommendations for delivering a safe, dignified humanitarian response that avoids revictimization. When an emergency or disaster strikes, institutional and community support networks weaken, livelihoods are disrupted, and pre-existing inequalities and vulnerabilities deepen. As a result, in crisis-affected settings, up to 70% of women experience violence, nearly double the rate recorded outside crisis zones. The challenge is even more urgent given global gaps in violence prevention and care. In 2025 alone, 50% of survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) were reported to lack access to essential services such as safe spaces, health care, psychosocial support, protection, or legal assistance, leaving at least one million women and girls without vital care. events.title: Cameroon Cholera Outbreak: Situation Report #8 (November 25, 2026)
events.summary: Country: Cameroon Source: International Medical Corps Please refer to the attached file. FAST FACTS 462 suspected cholera cases and four deaths (0.87% CFR) were recorded in Minawao Refugee Camp between July 24 and October 17, with zero new cases for 29 consecutive days as of November 15. Minawao hosts more than 81,000 refugees—more than triple its intended capacity (325%)—resulting in an attack rate of 570 cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Across Cameroon’s Far North Region, 3,038 cases (15% in Minawao) and 86 deaths (2.83% case-fatality rate) were recorded across 18 health districts as of November 9, with the last regional case reported on October 28. Though active cholera transmission inside Minawao has stopped, the wider regional outbreak has not yet been declared over. Overcrowding, cross-border mobility and unresolved water and sanitation gaps sustain the risk of reintroduction into the camp. OUR RESPONSE Operating in Minawao Refugee Camp since 2013, International Medical Corps launched an emergency cholera response within 24 hours of the initial alert on July 24, supporting the Mokolo Health District with pre-positioned contingency stocks. We expanded the camp’s existing 15-bed treatment unit to 100 beds using temporary overflow tents and 37 clinical and support staff. We trained, equipped and supervised 90 refugee community health workers (CHWs) across all camp blocks, who conducted 140,000+ household visits, traced 3,400+ contacts, and disinfected 8,000+ households and community spaces. Deployed all 90 CHWs as volunteer vaccinators—helping to reach 75,444 people (92.6% coverage)—and documented operational lessons to strengthen readiness for future outbreaks.

events.title: World: Protecting Children from Air Pollution: Applying the social and behaviour change message guidance in the REACH Framework
events.summary: Country: World Source: UN Children's Fund Please refer to the attached file. Highlights Air pollution is the single biggest environmental threat to child health. Around 930 million children, 4 in 10 worldwide, breathe outdoor air with a level of fine particles seven times that considered safe by the World Health Organization. Every day, almost 2,000 children under 5 years of age die from air-pollution-related causes, accounting for more than one in four of all deaths in this age group. Three quarters of these deaths are linked to air pollution inside the home. Yet it's one of the hardest risks to communicate, because the harm is invisible, cumulative, and easily normalized. This new guide offers a framework for messages that move families and decision makers from awareness to sustained protective action, organized around the REACH (recognize, engage, act, context, habit) framework and designed to be localized to each setting.
